Copied Arbitrum bridge on PulseChain: recorded activity and
token compatibility
Research date: 29 September 2026. This study is retrospective and read-only. It examines existing state,
logs, receipts and published contract source. It does not perform simulated privileged calls,
impersonation or transactions.
Findings
The copied Arbitrum contracts have a demonstrable post-fork transaction history. The bridge proxy
administrator changed owners twice, the custom gateway changed implementation and changed back,
and the rollup recorded node confirmations. Several custom-gateway withdrawals have corresponding
stablecoin transfers out of escrow in successful receipts. These observations establish activity and
specific control changes. They do not identify the humans behind addresses or establish that the
withdrawn assets originated from new native-L2 deposits.
The more specific claim about ARB has direct transaction support: on 21 September 2024, the copied
ARB token minted to a recipient during a successful outbox/gateway transaction. The mint, withdrawal
finalization and outbox execution occur in the same receipt. This proves the destination ARB mint
occurred; the source escrow balance has not been independently established.
A native-L2 lock/L1 mint bridge is a real contract pattern. In the reviewed Arbitrum reverse-custom
implementation, L2 tokens are transferred into escrow and the L1 gateway invokes the destination
token's bridgeMint. This can represent transferable ERC-20-compatible tokens, including suitable vault
shares. It is not a universal permission to mint every existing L1 token. The observed mappings for
OUSD, mUSD, eUSD and FRAX point to the ordinary standard gateway, not a reverse-mint gateway.
pDAI stabilization thesis · 4 October 2026 50

Evidence boundary
All state conclusions use chain 369, block 27,659,393, hash 
0xc5e582cd902f4bff3b1aa325b9b564fcd5d6dc0ffa77a03fcd105b65c6390275. Historical log searches run from block 
17,233,000 through that endpoint. This boundary follows the inherited Ethereum snapshot at block
17,232,999 reported by the PulseChain mainnet repository. Thus these observations distinguish post-fork
activity from inherited Ethereum logs. Block timestamps below are UTC.
The source is https://rpc.pulsechain.com; responses are saved under ignored artifacts/parb-bridge-
observations-20260929/. The endpoint block hash was re-read and matched. Logs carry their own block/
transaction hashes. Receipts for the specifically cited ownership changes, upgrades and withdrawals
report success. This is one-RPC evidence, not independent consensus verification.
The named-contract search is bounded: router, standard/custom/DAI gateways, ARB gateway, proxy
administrator and rollup were queried across the stated range. A query returning no logs does not prove
that no relevant transaction occurred anywhere, that no unlogged storage mutation occurred, or that a
distinct gateway does not exist. No actual pARB execution RPC or complete source deployment
catalogue has been established. An L1 counterpart address is not proof of a running source contract at
that address.

Both upgrade transactions have sender 0xb8698cfffdaaf26ca21fe8aa560c18cc2b2f5996. The second
implementation is also the pinned endpoint's implementation. Consequently, reading only the endpoint
would miss an intervening implementation change. The temporary implementation's complete behavior
and all intermediate storage effects are not established by these events alone. They are evidence of an
upgrade sequence, not evidence of a particular mint mechanism or beneficial/harmful intent.
pDAI stabilization thesis · 4 October 2026 51

The router returned no logs in the searched post-fork interval. Its owner and the custom gateway's
owner at the endpoint remain 0x3fffbadaf827559da092217e474760e2b2c3cedd, a separate role from proxy-admin
ownership. Treating these different authority layers as one owner would hide the observed distinction.

These are transfers from existing escrow, not zero-address mint events. Their token-unit sizes do not
establish dollar value. The custom gateway's two other returned withdrawal events occur in one
transaction at block 27,434,939 and identify token addresses 0xc08512927d12348f6620a698105e1baac6ecd911 and
0x58b6a8a3302369daec383334672404ee733ab239. Their source positions and token metadata have not been
classified in this study.
The copied rollup returned 265 NodeConfirmed events during the searched interval. The last records node 
5355, block 27,434,764, transaction 0x029d…83ea, consistent with the endpoint's latestConfirmed() value.
Confirmation is a specific L1 observation. The event does not disclose every source account or prove the
thesis's asserted trillion-token deposits. Neither node confirmations nor the observed withdrawals, by
themselves, demonstrate native-L2 receipt locking followed by minting an existing L1 OUSD, mUSD,
eUSD or aT oken.
ARB: an observed destination mint through the reverse gateway
The copied L1 ARB token is 0xb50721bcf8d664c30412cfbc6cf7a15145234ad1. At the endpoint, the router selects
gateway 0xbbce8aa77782f13d4202a230d978f361b011db27, whose reported counterpart is 
0xcad7828a19b363a2b44717afb1786b5196974d8e. These are distinct from the standard and custom escrow
gateways used by the named stablecoins.
The gateway's post-fork log query returns one WithdrawalFinalized event: transaction 0xeebae5…1968a, block 
21,469,490, 2024-09-21 11:15:05 UTC, block hash 
0xbbcb9b58dce7934e35e967f4b96f8810c8d47625ffe6490eb4b1cffdbe195f60. Its receipt reports success and contains, in
order:
An outbox execution event identifying the ARB gateway and its counterpart.1. 
pDAI stabilization thesis · 4 October 2026 52

An ARB Transfer from the zero address to 0x42543853a72edb6f1ff9bddab0cf4676187ec28a.
A WithdrawalFinalized event emitted by the ARB gateway for the same token, recipient and amount.
A bridge call event naming the outbox and ARB gateway.
The transaction sender is the recipient above; its direct target is the copied outbox 
0x0b9857ae2d4a3dbe74ffe1d7df045bb7f96e4840. This receipt supports the claim that ARB was minted on
PulseChain through the copied Arbitrum messaging and gateway path. It does not establish an
independently observed source escrow deposit or prove that every destination claim is backed by a
redeemable source position. This distinction remains necessary even when the L1 transaction succeeds.
The token reports 18 decimals. totalSupply() at block 21,469,489 is 6,903,225.677772492555339246
ARB. At block 21,469,490 it is 972,406,600,390,402,296,078,733,787,224.655675065021335672
ARB. The increase is exactly the receipt's zero-address transfer amount: 
972,406,600,390,402,296,078,726,883,998.977902572465996426 ARB. This reconciles an actual
token supply increase, not merely an event bearing a bridge-related name. The size alone says nothing
about redeemability or value. The preceding block's hash is 
0x03b8e9e8a7329b97e1a050628b156a530e013f3259a05109bb15b8ef939c0e75. The token implementation at the mint
block matches the endpoint implementation identified below.
Published L1ArbitrumT oken source contains bridgeMint and bridgeBurn restricted to arbOneGateway. This is an
explicit token-level integration, explaining why the ARB example cannot be generalized to an arbitrary
existing ERC-20 or existing Aave receipt. The destination token implementation read at the endpoint is 
0xad0c361ef902a7d9851ca7dcc85535da2d3c6fc7; the ARB gateway implementation is 
0x4e8c24617c4592895d52ac6df29d9647e9d01bb5. The token's arbOneGateway() getter matches the router-selected
gateway. Explorer-verified implementations identify L1ArbitrumT oken and 
L1ForceOnlyReverseCustomGateway. The latter disables ordinary token self-registration. Its reverse-
gateway inheritance implements destination minting, but its existence is not a permissionless mint
service for every token standard or every pool coin.
Source-message provenance of the ARB mint
A further bounded audit decodes the metadata in the already recorded ARB transaction using the 
executeTransaction parameter order in the published Outbox implementation. The transaction supplies
counterpart sender 0xcad7828a19b363a2b44717afb1786b5196974d8e, destination 
0xbbce8aa77782f13d4202a230d978f361b011db27, and message index 86. The successful historical trace's L2-
sender getter agrees with that counterpart.
Its l2Block, l1Block and l2Timestamp fields all contain the identical integer 
1072187306136427181113590999908369971006187625255, whose hexadecimal representation
is the destination gateway address. These fields therefore do not provide plausible source block numbers
or a calendar timestamp. Comparing the raw integer numerically with the fork block or Unix time would
misleadingly label the message as far-future; it cannot establish an actual post-fork source history. This
differs from the MIM transaction below, whose metadata describes ordinary pre-fork block/time values.
The destination execution date, 21 September 2024, is independently established by its PulseChain
block. The claim that the corresponding source deposit or lock occurred before or after the fork is not
established by the ARB message's supplied metadata. A successful destination mint is not a substitute
for a separately observed source lock.
The latest NodeConfirmed event in the existing rollup inventory before this mint is node 5253, block 
21,462,914, transaction 0x6127…dd00. This establishes temporal ordering only. The existing receipt and
call trace do not directly name that node as the mint's message provenance, and this audit does not
assert a root-to-message linkage from proximity. It has not reconstructed or replayed any message.

Decoded fields and the five nearest prior confirmation events are preserved separately in artifacts/parb-
arb-provenance-20260929/recorded_metadata.json, referencing the previously saved transaction hash, block
hash and raw input. This audit performed only interpretation of existing read-only evidence; it made no
configuration changes or simulated calls.
Public MIM transaction and historical call traces
The supplied transaction 0xa2e5…227d is successful at block 27,256,598, 2026-08-11 00:51:35 UTC,
hash 0x030fa534e9ffaa60decec678e56d76f627d84ad7dbfb545101d01fdc06620887. Its sender and token recipient are the
now-specified e121 wallet, 0x98c89980d1eae247ada3636ae27648f78e66e121. The token 
0x99d8a9c45b2eca8864373a26d1459e3dff1e17f3 reports symbol MIM and 18 decimals at this transaction's block.
The receipt records 152.747067838559905107 MIM transferred from the standard gateway 
0xa3a7b6f88361f48403514059f1f16c8e78d60eec to e121, alongside its withdrawal finalization and outbox
execution events. The token transfer originates from the gateway, not the zero address.
The public RPC's trace_transaction method returned the actual historical execution trees for both this
transaction and the ARB mint. These sharpen the receipt-only distinction:

gateway → MIM

The MIM trace contains 15 frames including proxy delegation and authentication reads. Its gateway
queries the inbox's bridge, the bridge's active outbox and the outbox's L2 sender; the latter returns
counterpart 0x09e9222e96e7b4ae2a407b98d48e330053351eee. The ARB trace contains 16 frames; its corresponding
L2 sender read returns 0xcad7828a19b363a2b44717afb1786b5196974d8e. The ARB token call is actually bridgeMint,
not an inference based only on the transfer event's appearance. Neither transaction's call tree contains
an Aave, Balancer or Curve call.
The existing MIM transaction's decoded outbox message metadata references L2 block 85,474,848, L1
block 17,151,178, and L2 timestamp 2023-04-29 10:32:06 UTC. That metadata predates the
inherited Ethereum snapshot. The transaction is therefore consistent with later execution of an inherited
withdrawal message; it is not evidence of a new post-fork pARB deposit or staking position. The source
block and its underlying receipt have not been independently obtained, so this conclusion does not
promote the message's supplied metadata into a separately verified L2 history.
These two cases demonstrate different destination mechanics in actual records. MIM supplies an exact
link between the named e121 wallet and the copied Arbitrum bridge. ARB supplies an exact existing-
token mint through its dedicated reverse integration. Neither transaction, considered alone, establishes
the broader Aave receipt → Balancer → DAI sequence or the source lock that would back every newly
issued representation. No real-person attribution follows from either sender address.
The public Otter trace pages could not be read in this environment (HTTP 403); debug_traceTransaction was
unavailable on the RPC. The successful trace_transaction responses provide the execution evidence
instead. These provider limitations were not interpreted as empty or failed transactions. New raw results
are kept separately under artifacts/parb-bridge-leads-20260929/, particularly mim_parity_trace.json, 
arb_parity_trace.json, the transaction/receipt pair, and MIM block/metadata reads. No live or locally
simulated transaction was sent.

The standard gateway's balances of those four stablecoins were zero at the endpoint; the custom
gateway's USDC balance was one USDC. A standard fallback mapping does not prove a source token has
been deployed or registered, nor that a destination mint function exists. No positive reverse-gateway
deployment and registration for these named existing pool coins has been demonstrated in this bounded
investigation.
What a reverse lock-and-mint bridge represents
The historical L2 reverse custom gateway uses safeTransferFrom and measures the change in its own token
balance. The historical L1 reverse custom gateway uses bridgeMint for the incoming destination
representation and bridgeBurn for its outgoing return. The L2 return operation transfers escrowed tokens
out. This establishes the lock/mint and burn/release direction from executable source. The files' header
comments contain a contradictory direction description; the function bodies, rather than that comment,
support this interpretation.
For ordinary non-rebasing shares, the relevant backing unit can be the locked share, rather than an
amount of underlying cash released on L1. A minted L1 share representation can be backed by a locked
L2 share without L1 underlying escrow. That fact still does not give it the local vault's share-token
identity or local underlying redemption rights. A source share, a new destination representation, and an
existing destination vault share are three distinct contracts unless an actual integration establishes the
intended relationship.
The L1 gateway authentication checks both the bridge caller and the outbox-reported counterpart
sender. Separately, the destination token must permit the gateway's mint/burn operations. Bridge
authority and token issuer authority are different checks. A new representation may implement the
required interface; an existing pool coin does not acquire it simply by sharing a name, address on
another chain, or an ERC-20 interface.
Token standards and receipts
“PRC-20” in this context describes ERC-20-style tokens on PulseChain; the name does not add cross-
chain issuance authority. The tokenized-vault standard relevant to the “4621” reference is ERC-4626.
This study does not identify an ERC-4621 bridge class.

The primary standards are ERC-20, ERC-4626, ERC-721, and ERC-1155. ERC-4626 requires ERC-20 share
behavior but permits nontransferable implementations to revert transfers; therefore even the ERC-4626
label alone is insufficient to demonstrate escrow compatibility. ERC-4626 asset/share conversions also do
not imply immediate redemption liquidity or external-dollar backing.
Interpretation and reproduction references
The public trail supports the proposition that copied infrastructure continued to process recorded actions
and underwent specific administrator and implementation changes, including the documented
destination ARB mint. It presently does not connect those events into the asserted complete source-
deposit → native receipt lock → exact L1 stablecoin mint → pool purchase sequence. The difference is
evidentiary: the source contracts, locked positions and authenticated messages for that specific
sequence have not been identified.
The returned logs are saved as router_rpc_logs.json, custom_rpc_logs.json, proxyadmin_rpc_logs.json and 
rollup_rpc_logs.json; each stores the exact request and response. event_receipts.json and 
event_receipts_retry.json store transaction, receipt, block and event-signature reads. Some initial requests
timed out; the successful retries are kept separately rather than overwriting failures. Full event

inventories and source copies remain in ignored artifacts, while this note retains only material findings.
The ARB case additionally uses arb_gateway_logs.json, arb_mint_receipt.json, arb_mint_tx.json, 
arb_mint_block.json, arb_mint_supply_before.json, arb_mint_supply_after.json, arb_token_gateway.json and the two
verified implementation source responses. The unfiltered ARB mint-event query returned an unreadable
response; the successful gateway log query and exact receipt establish the cited event without treating
that failed query as an empty result. standard_rpc_logs.json contains 93 returned withdrawal events and 
dai_gateway_rpc_logs.json contains two. These wider event inventories have not each been promoted to a
receipt-level interpretation in this bounded note.
Reproduction uses eth_getLogs with the stated address and inclusive block range, eth_getTransactionReceipt
for the cited hashes, and eth_getBlockByNumber for each event block and the endpoint. Event signatures
were checked with web3_sha3, not guessed from a display label. Endpoint mapping and balance calls are
preserved in artifacts/parb-validation-20260928/contracts.json and can be repeated with the existing read-
only Research/scripts/probe_pulsechain_routes.py scanner. No transaction-writing method was called in this
study.

What a reverse lock-and-mint bridge represents
The historical L2 reverse custom gateway uses safeTransferFrom and measures the change in its own token
balance. The historical L1 reverse custom gateway uses bridgeMint for the incoming destination
representation and bridgeBurn for its outgoing return. The L2 return operation transfers escrowed tokens
out. This establishes the lock/mint and burn/release direction from executable source. The files' header
comments contain a contradictory direction description; the function bodies, rather than that comment,
support this interpretation.
For ordinary non-rebasing shares, the relevant backing unit can be the locked share, rather than an
amount of underlying cash released on L1. A minted L1 share representation can be backed by a locked
L2 share without L1 underlying escrow. That fact still does not give it the local vault's share-token
identity or local underlying redemption rights. A source share, a new destination representation, and an
existing destination vault share are three distinct contracts unless an actual integration establishes the
intended relationship.
The L1 gateway authentication checks both the bridge caller and the outbox-reported counterpart
sender. Separately, the destination token must permit the gateway's mint/burn operations. Bridge
authority and token issuer authority are different checks. A new representation may implement the
required interface; an existing pool coin does not acquire it simply by sharing a name, address on
another chain, or an ERC-20 interface.
Token standards and receipts
“PRC-20” in this context describes ERC-20-style tokens on PulseChain; the name does not add cross-
chain issuance authority. The tokenized-vault standard relevant to the “4621” reference is ERC-4626.
This study does not identify an ERC-4621 bridge class.
